controls.notes: Tower centerline to tower centerline. SRC-002 dimensions it `1595'-6" MAIN SPAN`; SRC-001 gives 1,595.5 ft; SRC-003 "the bridge's 1,595.5-foot span broke all world records for span length".
SRC-002 labels both `930' LAND SPAN`. Independently in SRC-004's 1876 wire specification: "two side spans of 930 ft. each".
"Length of bridge proper". Identity holds exactly: CTL-001 + 2 × CTL-002 = 3455.5. Checked at build time.
SRC-002: "OVERALL LENGTH OF BROOKLYN BRIDGE FROM PARK ROW, MANHATTAN, TO ADAMS ST., BROOKLYN, 5989 FT. (1996.3 YD)".
`1562'-6" MANHATTAN APPROACH`. **The approaches are asymmetric and both are dimensioned**, so no 50/50 split is guessed anywhere in this model.
`971' BROOKLYN APPROACH`. Identity holds exactly: CTL-005 + CTL-002 + CTL-001 + CTL-002 + CTL-006 = 5989 = CTL-004. Checked at build time; this is the strongest single internal check in the document.

SRC-002 dimensions `135' MID SPAN CLEARANCE` directly off its `MEAN HIGH WATER` baseline. SRC-001: "Clear hgt. at mid-span above high water (90F) 135.0 ft." — the 90 °F qualifier is the thermal state at which the design clearance holds.

`110' CLEARANCE TO WATERLINE`, dimensioned from the `MEAN HIGH WATER` baseline up to the `ROADWAY` line at the Manhattan tower. It is **lower** than the 135 ft midspan clearance because the Brooklyn Bridge deck crests at the centre of the main span rather than sagging toward it — SRC-002's elevation draws that camber plainly. Used as the datum for the tower arch, see §4.2.
Park Row curb line, the Manhattan end of the approach.
Adams Street curb line, the Brooklyn end of the approach.
SRC-002: "3'-3" per hundred feet". SRC-001: "Grade of roadway 3.25%". Two sources, same number, expressed differently.
"THE BROOKLYN APPROACH REQUIRES A GRADIENT OF ONLY 1'-9" PER HUNDRED FEET."
`60' MID CHANNEL DEPTH`. Context for the river bed, not bridge structure.
"1950' OVERALL WIDTH EAST RIVER CHANNEL". Context only.
**ACTIVE tower height control.** SRC-002: `276'-6" OVERALL TO WATERLINE`. SRC-003: "the 276.5-foot towers". See CONF-001.
SRC-001's figure. Recorded for traceability, **not used for geometry**; see CONF-001, where it is shown to be a decimalisation error for 276'-6".
Tower masonry along the bridge axis at the mean high water line, dimensioned on the `ELEVATION TO EAST RIVER` view.
Tower masonry transverse to the bridge at the mean high water line, dimensioned on the `ELEVATION TO MANHATTAN` view. Wider than the 85 ft deck, as expected.
Manhattan and Brooklyn.

SRC-002: `33'-9" ARCH WIDTH`. SRC-004: "a span of 33 feet 9 inches". SRC-001 gives 33.8 ft, the same figure decimalised. Three sources.
"…and a width of 21 feet", i.e. the through-thickness of the arch along the bridge axis.
`46' RADIUS`, annotated on the pointed arch of the Manhattan tower.
SRC-002: `117' VAULT`, from the roadway line to the crown. SRC-001: "Height of arches above roadway 117.0 ft."
`36' ARCH HEIGHT`, measured from the springing course. **ACTIVE** for the arch derivation. See CONF-004.

**Scaled off the drawing, not stated on it.** Measured as a *ratio* on the orthographic elevation, so it is independent of any scale error: `(cable_y − towertop_y) / (MHW_y − towertop_y) × 276.5`. Both towers agree — Brooklyn 32 px below a 605 px tower, Manhattan 30 px below 580 px — giving 14.5 ft. The measurement chain is validated by a figure that played no part in setting it: the same scale puts the midspan deck underside at 133.9 ft against the drawing's own stated 135 ft. Graded `B`: grade-`A` material, but the scaling is this repository's derivation and a line on that sheet is about 5 ft thick. **Replaces a 0 ft placeholder, and supersedes a first attempt at 16.5 ft that mistook the flagstaff for the masonry cap.**
"two pointed arches which have a rise of 35 feet 6 inches". Recorded, **not used for geometry**. See CONF-004.

"the summit of the New York tower is 345 feet above the foundation". Recorded, **not used for geometry** — SRC-004 does not say which surface it calls the foundation, and the arithmetic against CTL-020 and CTL-034 does not close. See OQ-004.
SRC-002: "THE BROOKLYN CAISSON RESTS AT 44'-6"". SRC-001: 44.5 ft.

SRC-002: "THE CAISSON BELOW THE MANHATTAN TOWER COMES TO REST AT 78'-6"". SRC-001: 78.5 ft. **The two towers' foundations are at different depths and the model reflects that**; it does not average them.
"The dimensions of the caisson are rectangular, length one hundred and sixty-eight feet, width one hundred and two feet".
Same passage; SRC-005 gives 102 ft for both caissons.

"The dimensions of the base are one hundred and seventy-two feet by one hundred and two feet, covering an area of seventeen thousand five hundred and forty-four square feet. Its length is four feet greater than the Brooklyn caisson." 172 × 102 = 17,544 exactly — the source checks against itself.
"height of air chamber nine feet six inches".
"making the roof of the caisson a solid mass of timber, of fifteen feet in thickness".
SRC-002: "FOUR MAIN CABLES CARRY THE DEAD AND LIVE LOADS OF THE SUPERSTRUCTURE."
SRC-002: "the main cables reached their bound diameters of 15-3/4 inches". SRC-001: "Diameter over wrapping 15.75 in." See CONF-003.
"Length of each cable". Includes the anchorage-embedded run; see the arc-length cross-check in §4.4.
SRC-002: "THE FOUR MAIN BRIDGE CABLES WERE EACH COMPOSED OF 5,434 CONTINUOUS STEEL WIRES." See CONF-002.
"Total number of vertical suspenders 1,520".

"Total number of diagonal stays 400". The stays are the Roebling system's defining second load path; SRC-002 annotates them: "DIAGONAL STAY CABLES CARRY PART OF THE SUSPENDED SUPERSTRUCTURE (THE DECK LOAD)."
"THE MAIN CABLES WERE CARRIED THROUGH THE TOWERS ON EIGHT CAST IRON SADDLE BEARINGS OF 13 TONS EACH." Four cables × two towers.
Design-stage specification. Recorded, **not used**. See CONF-002.
Design-stage specification. Recorded, **not used**. See CONF-003.

Same sentence.

Brooklyn anchorage, "brought up to 78 feet 6 inches above high water". A **state of works**, not a finished height. Recorded, not used. See CONF-005.

SRC-001: "Average size of eyebars 12ft. x 3 in. x 8 in." SRC-002: "EIGHT LONG CHAINS OF 12-FOOT EYEBARS".
SRC-001: "Clear width of bridge 85.0 ft." SRC-002 labels the deck `85' BRIDGE FLOOR` on the plan.
One foot wider than the clear deck width, as expected for a beam carrying it.
SRC-003 quotes John Roebling's 1854 proposal directly: "…I have provided six lines of trusses."
"Height of inner and intermediate trusses 17.0 ft."
"Height of outer trusses 8.7 ft." The original outer trusses were half the depth of the inner ones.

SRC-001 note 2: "In the 1953 reconstruction of the suspended superstructure, the intermediate trusses were removed and the outer trusses were raised to the height of the inner trusses." All surviving trusses are therefore 17 ft deep.

**Reasoned, not stated.** Six trusses comprise two outer, two intermediate and two inner; SRC-001 note 2 says the intermediates were removed, leaving four. No read source states the number `4`. Graded `B` and flagged: see OQ-010.
"a 15-foot-wide walkway", describing the original 1883 deck division. The present-day widths are CTL-088 to CTL-095 and are quite different.
"Concrete Approaches - 2365 feet: 35%". Both ends combined.
"Wood Deck Approaches - 750 feet: 11%".
"Wood Deck with Cables – 1,510 feet: 23%". The stretch where the main cables descend alongside the path.
"Tower Ramps - 540 feet: 8%". Four ramps, two at each tower.
"Towers - 109 feet: 2%". The passage through both towers.
"Crown – 355 feet: 5%". The high point at midspan.
"Trunk Cable Bases - 114 feet, 2%". Where the cables reach path level — the narrowest points on the bridge.

"Brooklyn Curve - 910 feet: 14%". **The section that carries the promenade past the bridge's Adams Street terminus toward Tillary Street and Boerum Place (SRC-012), and the section that holds the Washington Street staircase.** See CONF-007.
"1. CONCRETE APPROACHES 17'". The widest section.
"Width of 16' is generally acceptable for a shared use path."
"Cable supports connect inside of fence narrowing effective width of pathway 13'".
"Approaching tower, fence moves from outside of cables to inside, narrowing path further 12'".
"5. TOWERS 43'". The path opens out into the tower balconies.
"Narrowest point on bridge is at trunk cable bases where the path is 10'".
"8. BROOKLYN CURVE … 11'", annotated "Narrow path, excess space on north side of fence to accommodate staircase". **This is the sourced statement that puts the staircase in this section.**
"The majority of the wood deck is 4' below girders except at the towers and tower ramps" — 79% of the length. Independently in SRC-015.

The promenade sits 18 ft above the automobile lanes. **Graded `B`, not `A`**: no primary or owner document read here states it, and SRC-015 is tertiary. It supersedes a 12 ft placeholder. SRC-011's grade-`A` "4 ft below girders" (CTL-096) is the relationship that will replace this once a girder elevation is registered — see OQ-013.

Present-day. NYC DOT: the bridge "supports five lanes of vehicles (no trucks), a pedestrian promenade and protected bike lane". SRC-011's 2016 history page says six lanes; one was taken for the bike lane in 2021. See CTL-099.

September 2021: a two-way protected bike lane replaced the leftmost Manhattan-bound vehicle lane, and the promenade became **pedestrian-only**. Recorded as a date, not a dimension; it is what makes CTL-098 current rather than historic.

PLACEHOLDER. Transverse offset of the two inner stiffening trusses. Bounded above by CTL-104. See OQ-002.

PLACEHOLDER, but bounded and not arbitrary. The Brooklyn Curve descends past Adams Street toward Tillary/Boerum (SRC-011, SRC-012). Its 910 ft length is grade `A` (CTL-087); carrying it down at this bridge's own sourced Brooklyn approach gradient (CTL-015, 1.75%) gives 15.9 ft of fall. **The gradient is sourced, applying it here is reasoning.** See OQ-014.

The Brooklyn staircase down to Washington Street, and the Manhattan approach staircase. **Their existence and location are grade `A`/`B`** — SRC-011 annotates both as pinch points and puts the Brooklyn one in the Brooklyn Curve; SRC-012 and SRC-013 name the streets; SRC-014 is direct testimony. Only the *size* is a guess, which is exactly why these parts are `INFERRED` and not `ASSUMED`. See OQ-015.

materials.notes: Timber caisson filled with concrete after landing; SRC-005 describes the filling of the air chamber. Rendered as concrete.
SRC-002 annotates the coursing directly: "TOWER STONES IN THE VERTICAL COURSES ARE QUARRY FACED, WITH THE CORNERS DRAFT-CHISELED TO SQUARE." SRC-004 specifies granite and limestone by course.
SRC-004: granite corners, cornice and curtain arches, over limestone backing.
SRC-003: "the first time that galvanized steel wire was used in cable construction".

SRC-002: "EIGHT **CAST IRON** SADDLE BEARINGS OF 13 TONS EACH". Cast iron is not in the closed material vocabulary; `steel_structural` is its nearest member and the distinction is recorded here rather than lost.
SRC-003: "the suspension system was initially designed in iron, but was changed to steel".
No read source states the present wearing surface. Graded `D` deliberately; **this does not lower the geometry grade of any deck part**.

The Promenade decking is famously timber, and SRC-011 does call its sections "wood deck" — but that is a *typology name*, not a materials statement, and reading it as one would be exactly the over-claim this axis exists to prevent. Stays `D` until a source says what the planks are.
SRC-004 describes the Brooklyn approach as brick piers and arches; the Manhattan approach is not described in the passages read.
The staircases exist and are located (SRC-011 puts the Brooklyn one in the Brooklyn Curve; SRC-012 and SRC-013 name the streets; SRC-014 is direct testimony). Nothing read says what they are made of.

**Catch-all for reference geometry only.** Placed last, and deliberately mapped to `reference` so that a real structural part accidentally falling through reads as an obviously wrong ghost in the viewer rather than as plausible grey stone.
